titre: The Patent Sold for One Dollar
accroche: In 1922 in Toronto, four researchers turn a fatal diagnosis into a chronic disease; three sell the patent for a symbolic dollar
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 31, 1920, a young Canadian surgeon with no laboratory experience writes in his notebook an idea jotted down after reading an article: tie off the pancreatic ducts of a dog, wait for the digestive tissue to degenerate, then isolate what remains. This scribbled sentence will lead, in a little over a year, to the first effective treatment of a disease that had until then been fatal in short order.

## A Disease Without Treatment

Before 1922, a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes in a child is the equivalent of a death sentence: life expectancy is counted in months. The only known treatment, a near-total starvation diet, sometimes prolongs by a few years a life already reduced to exhaustion.

Frederick Banting obtains a research post at the University of Toronto, where John Macleod, head of the physiology laboratory, assigns him a student, Charles Best. During the summer of 1921, the two men tie off pancreatic ducts in dogs and produce a first extract, still too impure for human use.

## A First Failure, Then a Purification

In December 1921, the biochemist James Collip joins the team. On January 11, 1922, a first extract is injected into Leonard Thompson, 14, dying of diabetes at Toronto General Hospital: his blood sugar falls, but impurities cause sterile abscesses at the injection site. The treatment seems unusable as it stands.

Collip then takes up the biochemical purification of the extract. On January 23, 1922, a second injection, with the purified version, brings blood sugar down to normal within a day, without the complications of the first attempt. Leonard Thompson will live another thirteen years thanks to this treatment.

## A Patent Sold for One Dollar

Banting, Best, and Collip assign the Canadian patent for the manufacture of insulin to the University of Toronto for the symbolic sum of one dollar, by a deed signed on December 19, 1922, with the idea, documented by their correspondence with the university's leadership, that anyone should be able to prepare the extract without a lucrative monopoly slowing its spread. Banting had moreover first refused to have the patent filed in his own name, judging that a physician should not patent a medical discovery; he ended up accepting, on December 18, 1922, under pressure from American legal opinions requiring that the true inventor appear on the application.

Banting and Macleod receive the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, a decision that provokes an immediate controversy within the team itself: Banting judges that Best's merit has been overlooked and shares his half of the prize with him; Macleod does the same with Collip.

## What Remains

The story of insulin shifts something taken for granted: a major scientific discovery is almost never the work of a single name remembered by posterity. Here, the idea, the animal experimentation, the biochemical purification, and the laboratory's expertise come from four people with distinct roles, each necessary to the others, and the first clinical trial, contrary to the image of an immediate success, first failed.

repere.texte: The program for treating childhood diabetes set up by Frederick Banting and Gladys Boyd at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, where Banting joins the team in 1923, cut childhood diabetes mortality in half within a decade.

carte.punch: Three researchers assigned the Canadian insulin patent to their university for one dollar.
carte.idee: In 1922 in Toronto, Banting, Best, Macleod, and Collip turn type 1 diabetes, until then fatal in short order, into a treatable disease. Banting, Best, and Collip assign the patent to their university for a symbolic dollar, so that no monopoly would slow its spread.

quiz.question: What happened during the very first trial of the extract on Leonard Thompson, on January 11, 1922?
choix: The extract proved a complete and immediate success, with no complications
Blood sugar fell, but impurities caused abscesses, making the extract unusable as it stood
The injection was refused by the patient's family for religious reasons
The extract had absolutely no measurable effect on blood sugar
quiz.explication: The first extract, still impure, did lower blood sugar but caused sterile abscesses. It was Collip's purification, applied twelve days later, that made the treatment truly usable; the story of an immediate, flawless success is a simplification after the fact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who assigned the Canadian insulin patent to the University of Toronto for one dollar?
choix: Banting, Best, and Collip, but not Macleod
All four members of the team, Banting, Best, Collip, and Macleod
Macleod alone, as head of the physiology laboratory
The University of Toronto, which had filed it in its own name
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The deed signed on December 19, 1922 bears the names of Banting, Best, and Collip. Macleod, head of the physiology laboratory, was never a party to the patent, even though he shares with Banting the Nobel Prize awarded the following year.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who receives the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and how does the team react?
choix: All four researchers receive it together, with no one objecting
Banting and Best receive it, and Macleod publicly contests the choice
Banting and Macleod receive it, and each shares his portion with another
Collip receives it alone, for having purified the extract made injectable
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The prize goes to Banting and Macleod, which provokes an immediate controversy within the team. Banting, judging that Best's merit has been overlooked, shares his half with him, and Macleod does the same with Collip.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Banting at first refuse to have the patent filed in his name?
choix: Because he thought the discovery belonged entirely to Charles Best
Because Canadian law then forbade patenting a medicine
Because he feared being sued after the failure of the first injection
Because he judged that a physician should not patent a medical discovery
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Banting held that a physician should not patent a medical discovery. He ended up accepting, on December 18, 1922, under pressure from American legal opinions requiring that the true inventor appear on the application.
